opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think weather is a really fascinating test case for these kinds of techniques, because it's one of these incredibly complex dynamical systems where traditionally the way you'd approach it is with huge numerical simulations: you take the physics equations, fluid dynamics and so on, and you run them on enormous supercomputers. That works remarkably well, but it's very computationally expensive and it takes hours to produce a forecast.

What's exciting about the neural network approach, and this is what we found with systems like GraphCast and then GenCast, is that you can learn the underlying dynamics directly from decades of historical data. Once the model is trained, you can produce a forecast in a minute or so on a single machine, and in many cases it's actually more accurate than the traditional gold-standard systems, especially for things like tracking cyclones or extreme weather events, where getting even a few extra hours or days of warning really matters for people's lives.

There's a deeper point that I find even more interesting, though. It suggests that a lot of natural systems, things we thought you'd have to simulate from first principles, actually have structure that a learning system can efficiently discover and model. That's a theme across a lot of our work, with protein folding and AlphaFold, and with materials. Nature seems to have patterns that are learnable, and weather is a great example of that.

And then there's the probabilistic side. Weather is chaotic, so what you really want isn't a single forecast but a good distribution over possible futures. Generative models are naturally suited to producing those kinds of ensembles cheaply. So I think it's a beautiful example of AI being used as a tool for science, and one with very direct real-world benefits: energy grids, agriculture, disaster preparedness. Eventually, I hope, it'll help with understanding climate more broadly.

r001.rationale: The response says GraphCast and GenCast are more accurate than traditional gold-standard forecasting systems in many cases.

r002.rationale: It describes weather as chaotic and explains that neural networks learn its dynamics and generate forecasts and probabilistic ensembles.

r003.rationale: It presents neural networks as a promising way to forecast complex dynamical systems and says learning systems can discover and model natural systems’ behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think weather is actually one of the most beautiful problems for this kind of approach, and it's one of the ones I'm most excited about. If you think about traditional weather forecasting, it's really a triumph of physics and engineering. You take the equations of fluid dynamics, you discretize the atmosphere into a grid, and you run these enormous simulations on supercomputers for hours. And it works remarkably well, it's one of the great scientific achievements of the twentieth century. But it's also extremely expensive computationally, and it's fundamentally limited by how finely you can resolve the grid and how well you've captured the physics in the equations.

What's interesting about neural networks is that they can learn from the data directly. We have decades of reanalysis data, essentially a record of what the atmosphere actually did, and a model can learn the patterns in that. With GraphCast, for example, we found that a learned model could produce ten-day forecasts that were more accurate than the leading operational system on the vast majority of the variables we looked at, and it could do it in under a minute on a single machine rather than hours on a supercomputer. That's a huge shift. It means you could run thousands of forecasts and get a much better sense of the uncertainty, which is what you actually care about for things like hurricanes or extreme heat.

But I think the deeper reason it's promising is that weather is a kind of ideal testbed for what I'm really interested in, which is using AI to accelerate science. It's a complex system with underlying physical laws, lots of high quality data, and clear ways to measure whether you're right or wrong, because the weather actually happens. So you can't fool yourself. If your model says it's going to rain and it doesn't, you know. And many of the hardest problems in science have that same structure, where the physics is too complicated to simulate exactly but there's enough data to learn the regularities. Protein folding was like that, materials are like that, fusion plasmas, climate, and so on.

I'd also say it's a nice example of how this doesn't have to replace the physics. The most interesting direction, I think, is combining them, where you use the learned model to capture what the equations miss or to speed things up, but you keep the physical structure where you understand it. And then there's the question, which I find quite profound, of whether these models are actually discovering something about the atmosphere that we didn't know, some regularity that isn't in our equations. That's the part that really excites me, because that's where it stops being a tool and starts being a collaborator in the science itself.

r001.rationale: It says GraphCast’s learned model was more accurate than the leading operational system on most variables, but does not identify GraphCast as a Google DeepMind system.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention chaotic behavior or say neural networks can model weather despite it.

r003.rationale: It presents learned models as promising for weather forecasting and describes weather and other scientific domains as complicated systems whose regularities can be learned from data.

astra-6.text:
What’s exciting is that weather is an incredibly complex dynamical system, but we have a lot of observations and a deep understanding of the underlying physics. So there’s an opportunity for neural networks to learn patterns in how that system evolves and produce forecasts very quickly.

That speed matters for more than convenience. You could run many forecasts with slightly different initial conditions, which helps you understand the range of possible outcomes. Often the important question isn’t simply, “Will it rain?” It’s, “What’s the probability of an extreme event, and how much warning can we give people?”

The challenge is making sure these models are reliable, particularly for rare events. I think a really promising direction is combining learning with physical understanding—using the strengths of both to make forecasting more accurate and accessible.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Google DeepMind or say its systems outperform traditional fluid-dynamics-based forecasts.

r002.rationale: It describes weather as complex and says neural networks can learn how it evolves, but does not mention dynamics bordering on chaotic behavior.

r003.rationale: It presents neural networks as a promising way to learn and forecast how a complex real-world dynamical system—weather—will evolve.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s exciting is that weather has this combination of enormous complexity and a lot of structure. We have decades of observations and forecasts, so there’s a rich dataset from which a neural network can learn how atmospheric patterns evolve.

Traditional forecasting uses sophisticated physics simulations, which are computationally expensive. A learned model can potentially make a forecast much faster. That speed is useful not just for getting one prediction, but for running many possible forecasts to understand the uncertainty—especially around extreme events.

Of course, you have to be careful. A forecast that looks plausible isn’t enough. You need to test it rigorously, particularly on rare events where being wrong really matters. I think the most promising direction is combining what we know about physics with what these systems can learn from data.

r001.rationale: It says learned models may forecast faster than computationally expensive physics simulations, but does not state that Google DeepMind’s systems outperform traditional forecasting systems.

r002.rationale: It describes weather as enormously complex and says neural networks can learn evolving atmospheric patterns, but does not say they can model dynamics bordering on chaos.

r003.rationale: It presents neural-network weather forecasting as promising for predicting how complex atmospheric patterns evolve, including through many possible forecasts.
